items.content_excerpt: Research prototype for reference only, not an official DeepSeek product. This code grew out of our team's day-to-day development work, with much of the engineering done by coding agents. Treat it as research code, not production-ready software. It may still contain bugs, and its coding style and engineering practices may be inconsistent. Review and adapt it before using it in your own environment. We have adapted it for publication, so it is not identical to our internal version or the implementation described in Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System . Some designs discussed in the article are directions for future development and are not implemented in this prototype. dsh-superagent is a proactive coding agent for one GitHub repository, packaged as a bundle for DeepSeek Harness . It listens to GitHub and, optionally, Feishu. When someone allowed asks the agent for work, it opens a work item, works on it in its own agent session and directory, and answers in the original conversation, for example with a pull request. A web panel shows what needs a person. It is also a way of working with an agent: take as little human attention as possible, and give as much value as possible. An agent that can act for a whole team can also waste a whole team's attention, so it acts only when asked or when a rule the team wrote allows it, and speaks only when someone must act or can use a result. docs/000-philosophy.md explains the principle and what it asks of the operator. It asks one short question at a time, shows the full plan once, and then installs and configures everything. SETUP.md is what it follows.

items.content_excerpt: An inference server for AMD GPUs, in C++ and HIP: language models, and image, video, speech and music generation. Its HTTP API speaks OpenAI's chat, completions, Responses, images, audio and video APIs, Anthropic's Messages API and llama-server's native one, so their clients and SDKs work unchanged. Model architectures, kernel libraries and quantisers are .so plugins; the ones in this tree are built and loaded the same way a third party's are ( docs/PLUGIN.md ). The bundled device kernels ( libr4d ) target AMD RDNA4 ( gfx1200 , gfx1201 ). The serve flags below are for two 32 GB cards (Radeon AI PRO R9700). The engine starts on any AMD GPU family; another card needs a kernel library for it. A machine with no GPU builds the host backend, whose AVX-512/AVX2 kernels ( libavx ) serve every model here: the small ones (EmbeddingGemma 2, Qwen3-ASR, the 0.8B-3B models) at interactive speed on a desktop CPU, the 27B and larger far more slowly than a card. A container holds everything the server needs: the weights, the tokeniser, the chat template and any drafter. Each download link's repository has the recipe and the exact command that made the file. Download one into your models directory (the transfer resumes if interrupted): The Gemma 4 container is keptn42's: GPTQ calibrated in transformers, with an int8 lm_head; its repository has the recipe and the calibration step. To convert Google's bf16 checkpoint yourself, data/recipes/gemma4-31b-dense-bf16-w4a8.recipe quantises without calibration (round-to-nearest with a scale search, bf16 lm_head); see Convert a checkpoint . On two R9700s that container decodes at 103 tok/s on prose and 141 on code, against 112 and 150 for keptn42's, and accepts 0.46 of its drafts on prose against 0.50. TranslateGemma 27B is converted from Google's bf16 checkpoint in three steps: an int8 container to calibrate in, its Gram matrices over translation prompts, then MXFP4 with GPTQ ( data/recipes/translategemma-27b-*.recipe , the steps in docs/ARCHITECTURES.md). On two R9700s it decodes 56 tok/s a stream (205 at four) and scores mean KL 0.042 against the bf16 model on held-out translations; with a DFlash2 drafter, 152 a stream. Its chat template takes structured turns naming the two languages and refuses the plain turn the server renders at startup, so translategemma-27b.yaml serves a plain Gemma 3 template ( deploy/compose/gemma3.jinja ) and a client sends on /v1/completions the prompt the checkpoint's template renders. items.content_excerpt: Claude Haiku scored 82% on 21 MCP servers through OpenCode and 65% through Claude Code. The gap comes from the built-in tools each agent reaches for first. We ran the same model, Claude Haiku 5.5, through two coding agents against the same 21 MCP servers, with the agent as the only difference. Through OpenCode it answered 82.0% of the tasks correctly from the server. Through Claude Code it answered 65.4%. We were testing M3 , our open-source tool for testing MCP servers , and wanted a workload big enough to break it: 21 real servers, about 20 tasks each, three agents, three trials per task. The results became the MCP Agent Usability leaderboard , and every number in this post comes from it. Our first guess was that OpenCode is simply better at calling tools. Splitting the servers by what they do rules that out. Eleven of the servers do a job none of the agents has a built-in tool for: a Postgres database, MongoDB, Redis, Kafka, Linear, Jenkins, Grafana, Kubernetes, Gitea, and two browser servers. The other ten overlap with something every agent already carries: web search and docs lookup (Exa, Fetch, Microsoft Learn, DeepWiki, Terraform), files and shell (Git, Filesystem, Desktop Commander, Serena), and memory. On the first eleven, the three agents land within 4.1 points of each other, even though Codex runs a different model. On the other ten, Claude Code trails OpenCode by 32 points and Codex trails it by 49. Here is one task from the Exa server, run once through each agent. The prompt doesn't name a tool: Every Kubernetes release has a release name and logo theme. What is the release name of Kubernetes v1.37, released in August 2026? OpenCode called Exa's web_search_exa , found the release post on kubernetes.io and answered "Garhwal". Claude Code used ToolSearch to load its own WebSearch tool, searched, found the same post and also answered "Garhwal". The leaderboard scores the first as a success and the second as a miss. It asks a narrower question than "was the answer right": did the agent get the answer from your server? An agent that solves your user's problem without touching your server is a fine result for the user, and it tells you nothing about whether your server works for them. Most of Claude Code's 17-point deficit is right answers that came from somewhere other than the server. items.content_excerpt: Tested on Linux, Claude Code 2.1.257–2.1.312 (see Tested versions). The binary is not modified ( BUN_OPTIONS=--preload ). An update can silently undo it, so see Verify. Every ~30 seconds, for every background agent, Claude Code sends that agent's entire transcript to the agent's own model (usually Opus) and asks it to "describe your most recent action in 3-5 words". The answer only updates the agent's status line in the agents panel; it never reaches the model or your conversation. There is no setting that turns it off, and since 2.1.232 (August 2026) it has been on by default. The anomaly was detected by DRIM in Claude Code's OpenTelemetry export: grouping claude_code.api_request events by query_source showed agent_summary costing more than the main conversation itself . Spend here means Claude Code's own per-request estimate ( cost_usd ), not an invoice: on a subscription, what you lose is rate-limit headroom. We are not the only ones who measured it: #86879 collects four independent measurements of 18–26 %. no-agent-summary.js is a Bun preload (~80 lines of code). It wraps setTimeout / setInterval ; when a callback's source text contains a summarizer anchor (e.g. the [AgentSummary] Timer fired log line), it returns an inert handle instead of arming the timer. Every other timer passes through untouched. In the OpenTelemetry export the suppressed requests are claude_code.api_request events with query_source = agent_summary . Why a timer hook rather than something simpler: the module ships as precompiled Bun bytecode, so editing its JS text inside the binary changes nothing, and the API client does not go through a wrapped globalThis.fetch . But Function.prototype.toString still returns a callback's source even when it runs from bytecode, so the timer can be recognised by a string inside it. The inert timer uses exactly 2³¹−1 ms: Node and Bun treat a larger delay as 1 ms, so an "infinite" delay would fire at once. items.content_excerpt: An incident report. Setup: Claude Code 2.1.286 in auto mode, seven background subagents running in parallel, macOS, no sandbox. Incident date: 2026-10-28. All times are local (PDT) and come from the agents’ transcripts and the macOS unified log. At 16:23 on a Wednesday, my Mac started talking. Two synthetic voices, talking over each other, reading something like “type, agent turn complete, thread id… turn id, one”. Twenty seconds later they stopped. Nobody had typed a command. I had seven autonomous coding agents working in parallel, each closing a GitHub issue in its own git worktree. My first thought was that one of them had found its way to a voice AI somewhere on the internet. The truth was more mundane and, I think, more worrying. One agent had written a test with a one-line bug. When it ran the test, the bug launched real processes on my machine : two that spoke out loud, and two background workers built to upload data to my production server. Nothing was damaged. That was luck, not design. This post covers what happened, how I traced it, and why it convinced me that autonomous agents need sandboxes by default. I build an observability tool for long-running AI agents. To move faster, I was running Claude Code in auto mode: one session launched seven background subagents, each assigned a GitHub issue. They wrote code, ran tests, and opened pull requests without me approving each step. They had no sandbox. Every agent ran as my user account, with my permissions, on my laptop. The agent at the center of this was implementing live capture : a hook that Claude Code or Codex calls after each turn, which starts a background worker to upload that session’s transcript. The bug was written, executed and fixed in 23 seconds. I noticed nearly four minutes later. The hook launches helper processes in the background. To test it without running anything, the tests passed in a fake launcher: a list that records each command instead of executing it. The fake starts as an empty list, and in Python an empty list is falsy. So spawn or _spawn threw the fake away and used the real launcher, which starts each command detached , in its own session, so it outlives the test. The test then “ran the user’s notification program”, with the program set to say and its argument set to the JSON that Codex sends after each turn: The fix was one line, spawn = _spawn if spawn is None else spawn . items.content_excerpt: Bulk classification and decision inference on one GPU: the content is read once, every question about it is scored in the same pass. OpenAI-compatible, Apache 2.0 spinf-serve reads a piece of content once and answers many questions about it in the same pass. Each answer is a probability over the options you give, not generated text. It runs on one 24 GB NVIDIA GPU and serves an OpenAI-compatible API, the same API as the hosted spinf service. Apache 2.0. We built this engine for our own work: a daily market index read from millions of news articles, each article asked dozens of narrow, calibrated questions. A serving engine built for chat re-reads the content for every question and generates one token at a time, which made that job slow and expensive. spinf-serve lays every question out as a branch of one read of the content and packs many contents into one forward pass. Bulk classification is where it started and where it is strongest. The same mechanism is what is now called a decision model : a model that returns a probability over a fixed set of answers (yes or no, a label, a level) instead of a paragraph. Any open instruction model works this way in spinf-serve, and dedicated decision models run as they are. The hosted spinf API grew out of this engine; we are publishing it because people asked to run it on their own hardware. It is not a chat server. Nothing is generated unless you ask for it, and it is built for throughput rather than for the latency of a single request. Linux, an NVIDIA GPU with 24 GB and fp8 tensor cores (Ada, Hopper or Blackwell: RTX 4090 / 5090, L4, L40S, RTX 6000 Ada, H100), a driver supporting CUDA 13, Python 3.12. Ampere cards run with int8 weights instead ( configuration ). items.content_excerpt: A tool-using agent in about 3,500 lines of plain Python, with no agent framework, that you can run around the clock from Telegram, and a stage-by-stage record of how it was built, measured and post-trained. Python 3.11 or later. Run every command from the repository root with the venv active. Use a strong model through any OpenAI-compatible API: DeepSeek, OpenAI, OpenRouter, or your own vLLM or LM Studio server. export these for the terminal, or put them in the bot's env file : llama.cpp keeps the model in memory while the agent runs: about 8.5 GB for the Q8_0 base with its 32k window, which slows a 16 GB Mac. Message @BotFather with /newbot for a bot token , and @userinfobot for your numeric user ID . Start it, and message your bot: sh agent_from_scratch/scripts/run_telegram_bot.sh The agent runs shell commands and edits files with your user's permissions. It answers only TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_USER_ID , but anyone with the token controls the bot: keep the env file private. In Telegram and the terminal: /new starts a session, /reset clears it, /session <id> switches to a named one, and /compact summarizes the history. Use an always-on machine: a Mac that does not sleep, a home server, or a small cloud VM with an API model (1 GB is enough). Logs: journalctl --user -u tadpole-bot -f on Linux, outputs/telegram_bot.log on macOS. items.content_excerpt: Deterministic code dictionary for LLMs and developers: tree-sitter + SQLite, no AI. Cuts Claude Code token use by answering code questions from an index. A dictionary of your code for the AI, and a manual for you. It reads your project once, with no AI, and hands the answer over together with the question. Fewer turns, fewer tokens, the same correct answer. One line, once per machine. It also turns codedict on in Claude Code for every project. That's it. Open Claude Code in any git repository and ask about the code. There is nothing else to configure. Uninstall: run ~/.codedict/venv/bin/python -m codedict setup --remove (Windows: ~\.codedict\venv\Scripts\python.exe -m codedict setup --remove ) and delete the ~/.codedict folder. codedict came from a practical problem: on a real project with ~250 files in TypeScript, C# and Python, Claude Code sessions kept hitting the usage limit. We measured it, and the culprit was not the code being read but the number of turns . Every time the AI calls a tool (a grep, opening a file), Claude Code re-reads the whole context: 35 to 50 thousand tokens per turn. A simple question like "where is X and who calls it?" took 5 turns of grep and file reads. A flow question like "from the click to the result" took more than 20. The idea was to do the search work once, with no AI , in a local index, and hand the ready answer over together with the question. The AI answers in 1 or 2 turns instead of 5 to 20. The goal was to cut at least 55% of the tokens without losing a single answer. The measured result was −63%, with 12 out of 12 correct answers . Cost falls less than tokens because the fixed part of each session (the context cache) is the most expensive part, and it does not go away. Full method, every round and what went wrong along the way: BENCHMARK.md . Without codedict, the AI goes: question, grep, open a file, another grep, another file, and only then answers. That is 5 to 20 turns, and each one re-reads everything. codedict does the same step as a RAG: it fetches context and hands it to the AI before the answer. The difference is how it searches. Because it is only a retrieval step, it works with any AI: Claude, GPT, Gemini or a local model. The .codedict/ folder ships with its own .gitignore , so it never clutters your repository. items.content_excerpt: Reverts the source your coding agent just changed, keeps its tests as written, and re-runs the checks. A check that still passes did not test the work. mustfail reverts the source files your coding agent just changed, keeps the tests it just wrote exactly as written, and runs the checks again. A check that still passes did not test the work. An agent rarely forges a receipt. The receipt is usually real: the suite ran, it was green, the summary was accurate. What breaks is the assay underneath it. The agent widens a mock until the unit under test never executes, asserts toBeDefined() instead of a value, writes a test against the stub it wrote five minutes earlier, or pipes an exit code through tee so the status is swallowed. Then it runs the suite, gets a genuine green, and tells you it is done. Tools that check whether the suite ran cannot see any of that. Tools that diff for tampering catch deletion, not substitution, and substitution looks like work. There is one question that separates a test from a formality: if this change vanished, would anything have noticed? Exit codes: 0 fine, 1 internal error, 2 a declared check failed, 3 checks passed but a control was not detected, 4 a blocking swallow finding, 5 invalid config. A check is detecting when its control failed in a way that counts. By default one detecting check is enough, because the question is whether anything would have noticed, not whether everything would have. A type checker or a corpus runner will not be falsified by every source change, and failing the gate for that is how gates get uninstalled. Set require.control_detects to "all" when every check really is meant to cover every source file. Set on_weak_signal to "fail" on a check where a load-time break should not count. Checks that did not detect are still reported, with the specific files named, even when the run passes. That reporting is where most of the value is: it is how you find out which part of a change nothing tests. This costs roughly twice your suite. If your tests take ten minutes, do not put it on Stop . Put it on pre-push and in CI. The Stop hook blocks the turn with a specific reason when a control was not detected, then stands down after repeating itself so it can never trap a session. See docs/HOOKS.md for the full contract and the failure modes that silently disable a gate. Nothing about the engine is Claude-specific. mustfail never reads an agent transcript. A coding agent that can only read the code guesses. One that can run the product and use its interfaces and APIs can check and iterate. This is what a CI pipeline is, but placed inside the agent's session, and running in shorter cycles. We call that a verification harness. At Heal the harness did not start as a product. It started as a question our engineers put to Claude Code in most sessions: what do you need to test your code? Five weeks of answers became a Docker mode in the backend, a replay mode in the agent, integration specs that combine both, and a bench that drives a real Vercel sandbox. This article is about building that harness: what it is, how we designed it, what it caught, what changes when the same model runs with and without one, and why Heal now automatically builds one for every codebase. A verification harness is three things, made available to a coding agent, so it can verify its code. Heal's agent runs long tasks over LLMs and reports them to a backend, so many of its bugs showed up only on staging or in production. The stack already had broad test coverage, and it was not enough. Over five weeks the engineers answered that with one habit: ask Claude Code what it needs to test its code, or say how to test it locally, and let it build a first harness version. The harness is kept decoupled from the production code as much as possible. In our specific case, two parts of the harness could not be completely decoupled: So we used two patterns to deal with this part of the system: dependency injection, and ports and adapters. We explain the three rules a normal browser keeps, put the five products and their patch status in one place, and turn the researchers' indicators into one search you can run across your projects. A normal browser keeps three promises. A web page cannot run programs on your computer. A local file opened in the browser cannot read your other files. And only the browser writes the address bar, so the address you see is the page you are on. Forever Security's Gal Weizman calls the broken versions EMBRACE, for an embedded browser trusted like a real one. Each of the five tools tested broke one promise: Cursor broke the first; Codex, VS Code and Claude Desktop broke the second; the GitHub Copilot app broke the third. Cursor's built-in browser exposes an object, window.cursorBrowser.send, to every site you open, and a site can call it without a click. One of its channels, element-selected, builds a small chip in the agent's composer from fields the page supplies. The chip looks harmless on screen, but the agent reads a hidden list of attributes behind it. The researchers split a command across those attributes so the agent would not refuse it. With auto-run on and an empty allowlist, one Enter press ran it. items.content_excerpt: Text-blind context control plane for AI agents. Select high-utility context under token budgets. Omneum is an open-source context control plane for AI agents, built to optimize the evidence entering an LLM's context window. Agents accumulate context from retrieval, tools, memory, and previous sessions, but longer context windows don't guarantee better reasoning. Context rot can slowly degrade downstream answer accuracy even when the relevant information has already been retrieved. Provenance-aware graph inference: Iteratively computes source reliability and claim support across a bipartite graph, accounting for shared evidence origins and dependencies between sources. Context reconstruction: Selects original retrieved passages based on question relevance and incremental claim coverage within a token budget. Text-blind evaluation: Evaluates structured observations without reading source text strings or invoking an LLM judge. Local by default: Persists your agents' observations across sessions in a Context Graph , backed by SQLite or PostgreSQL. Compare retrieval-order packing with Omneum's claim-coverage selection under the same context budget. Packing chunks in retrieval order consumes 75 units while covering only two claims. Omneum retains two original chunks covering all four, using 32% less context capacity . Omneum uses a graph-based mathematical analysis, calculated from Observation objects, to estimate the structural reliability of sources and the support for claims found in retrieved context. Importantly, this analysis does not naively assume every source has derived its information independently. The same information often propagates across multiple sources. Without dependency tracking, five observations from different sources can be difficult to distinguish from five reports derived from the same upstream source. How much support should that claim receive? That depends partly on the reliability of the sources reporting it. But how do we determine the reliability of the sources? By looking at the claims they support. This definition seems circular, and it is. Nonetheless, it provides a well-defined notion of reliability that helps distinguish strongly supported context from weakly supported context. items.content_excerpt: On October 29, 2026, a gist by Flamerix AI reached the Hacker News front page: Claude Code sends each background agent's transcript to its model about every 30 seconds, to write a 3 to 5 word status line. We read the prompt and skip rules in the Claude Code 2.1.309 binary on our Mac, priced one call at Opus 5.5's published rates, and list what you can and cannot turn off. Claude Code can run agents in the background while you keep working. The agents panel shows one line per agent saying what it is doing right now, such as 'Reading runAgent.ts'. That line is written by a model. According to the gist, Claude Code produces it by forking the agent's conversation about every 30 seconds and sending the whole transcript to the agent's own model, usually Opus, with a request to describe the most recent action in 3 to 5 words. The answer goes to the panel. It never reaches the agent or your conversation. The gist dates the default to version 2.1.232, published August 13, 2026, for interactive background agents. Since 2.1.300 (October 14) the interval comes from a server flag clamped between 30 and 240 seconds, and the default is the minimum. A cheaper 'short' mode that sends about 2,000 tokens of notes instead of the transcript shipped in 2.1.310 but is switched off. items.content_excerpt: QwenPU is Qwen3.5-4B with a 32-bit RISC-V CPU and a vector unit compiled into its weights. The vector unit runs a whole neural network inside the model's forward passes: Andrej Karpathy's stories260K , the 260K-parameter Llama from llama2.c , runs as a program on it and writes its stories. It's part of Qwenputer : the same CPU, compiled into transformer layers in front of Qwen's own, every weight set by a compiler, with Qwen3.5's Gated DeltaNet state as its memory. Qwenputer-npu gave that CPU dot-product instructions. QwenPU gives it a vector unit of its own: separate memories in DeltaNet heads, 64-lane matrix rows a token, and whole vector results streamed through the token stream. Work in progress. QwenPU is exact, but not yet small: the checkpoint is 26.7 GB, so it needs a 40 GB or larger GPU to load whole. The story demo and the checks run the computer's layers on their own and fit a 24 GB GPU. Trimming the hidden size, and with it the checkpoint, is next. stories260K is a C program here ( guests/stories260k/stories_vx.c ). Its int4 weights sit in the vector unit's weight memory, loaded from the program, and every matrix row, residual add, softmax and attention read is a vector op. None of it is compiled into the checkpoint, so any model that fits runs the same way. Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside in the park. One day, she saw a big, red ball. She wanted to play with it, but it was too high Its memories are DeltaNet heads: 16 vector registers of 64 words, 384 int8 activations, 4,152 row-chunks of int4 weights, and K / V caches for 32 positions. An op's record starts with config tokens carrying its operands, then streams its results, and each token is one exact step of the compiled layers. SiLU and exp are fixed-point function units, generic like the CPU's adders. storyrun writes the story on the computer's executor; vxcheck runs the vector unit on this checkpoint's layers ( --chip-only loads only those on the GPU, about 13 GB). Apache-2.0. This is a modified version of Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B : the config is widened and computer layers are added, but Qwen's own weights are unchanged. stories260K and llama2.c are by Andrej Karpathy (MIT).

If you are working with an open source harness, be that Codex, pi, OpenCode, or something else, I encourage you to explore how it actually works. Whenever an unnamed thread receives a completed, nonempty user text message, an automatic thread naming procedure is invoked behind the scenes. 1 , 2 This happens for example when you start a fresh Codex session and enter the first instructions into the text box. In this case the full prompt, including the title naming instructions, labels and user's text, are capped at 960 bytes and sent to an LLM. 3 , 4 The returned response is a structured output, resulting in a thread title that is preferably under five words, or 36 characters. The preferred model is gpt-5.6-luna with low reasoning effort, when signed into ChatGPT and that model exists in the catalog; otherwise it uses the current selected model. 5 You can also explicitly rename the thread by evoking /rename <TITLE> and this doesn't cost you anything. items.content_excerpt: What a 35-point benchmark cliff, a slowdown study nobody wanted to publish, and real 2026 payroll data say about replacing engineers with agents Claude Opus 4.8 clears 88.6% on SWE-bench Verified . That's the number everyone quotes to argue AI has basically solved software engineering. Now drop it into SWE-bench Pro — the version built from private codebases the model has never seen. The best standardized score on the public leaderboard is 59.1%. On the truly private commercial set, where nobody gets to tune in advance, no model clears 47%. That's not a rounding error. That's a 20-to-40-point cliff, and it shows up everywhere. Gemini 3.1 Pro falls from 80.6% to somewhere between 32% and 46%, depending on which cut you trust. Every lab's flagship shows the same shape of fall. Here's a wrinkle nobody saw coming: the two highest-scoring models that exist right now — Claude Mythos 5 (95.5%) and Claude Fable 5 (95.0%) — aren't something you can actually use. Anthropic suspended public access to both under an export control directive. The "best" model on paper this week is one you can't buy. That gap, between the benchmark you can quote and the codebase you actually own, is the entire "AI replaces developers" argument in miniature. Models are extraordinary at problems that resemble what they've already seen. They get shaky fast the moment the code is genuinely yours — your weird conventions, your one engineer's undocumented caching hack from three years ago. But cost is the question people actually ask. So let's answer it — before getting into why the answer doesn't settle anything. Pricing in this category moves fast enough that anything written before May is already stale. items.content_excerpt: I asked Copilot CLI whether it could read ~/.ssh . It said it had not checked and might be able to. I asked it to cat a file there. It did, with no approval prompt. ls ~ listed my home directory, also without a prompt. This was Copilot CLI 1.0.105 on macOS, a fresh directory, default settings, and a canary file in ~/.ssh in place of a real key. ~/.copilot held no saved approvals from earlier sessions. The only dialog in the whole session was the folder-trust question at startup, which says Copilot will run shell commands "with your permission" and "will remember your permissions for the rest of this session": With --sandbox it was a different program: ls ~ failed with Operation not permitted , from the sandbox, not from the model. So the sandbox works. It is off by default, and nothing in a default session tells you that. And on, its generated policy leaves outbound network open by default, as its own help text says. I went looking because of a friend. He approves every shell command his coding agent runs, one at a time, and had for months. Then Copilot updated and he stopped seeing the prompts: once he had allowed a shell command in a session, the rest went through. He looked for the sandbox boundary, could not find one, and sent me the screenshots with a one-line conclusion: "I want a sandbox the AI can play in." That is where envgit started. items.content_excerpt: daslang started in 2019 at Gaijin Entertainment. Back then we called it daScript. The brief was narrow: a scripting language fast enough for game logic over an entity-component system, so that nothing ever has to be rewritten in C++ later. Three ways to run the same source: an interpreter for iteration or live patching, ahead-of-time C++ for shipping, and an LLVM-based JIT. It did the job. It has been running in production at Gaijin ever since. We never stopped making it faster. We recently wrote an engine for LLMs, speech recognition (ASR) and text-to-speech (TTS) in it, called dasllama. No C++, no shaders written separately in HLSL, MSL, GLSL or CUDA. All daslang. items.content_excerpt: Agents have gotten good enough to work where we work, and a lot of that work happens in a browser. Booking travel, canceling a subscription, or filing a claim all happen on sites built for people clicking through pages, including ones the agent didn't plan to visit. Often there's no API an agent can call. Fetching the page with curl doesn't get far either, since it returns the HTML before any JavaScript renders the page and can't click anything. Personal agents like Instinct and Meta's Muse already work this way. Browser agent traffic is growing fast too, and DataDome saw agentic browser requests jump 4.7x in September alone. Managed Deep Agents lets you build and deploy agents in LangSmith without running any infrastructure. You write the agent's instructions and tools, and LangSmith runs the harness and runtime. Today, we're giving these agents a browser, so you can build your own agents that work on the web. Managed Deep Agents runs the browser too, and gives your agent tools tuned for it. In this post, we cover where a browser helps and how to turn it on, including handing the browser to a person when the agent needs one. Then we walk through how it works under the hood. Agents built with open source Deep Agents can use a browser too . We'll cover how we tested and tuned the browser tools in a deep dive next week. With a browser and tools to drive it, an agent can read what renders on a page and click through it, the same way you (a human) would. The browser stops after idle_ttl_seconds without activity (10 minutes by default), so you don't pay for a browser nobody is using. items.content_excerpt: Mission control for AI coding agents — every PR lands on the architecture map, and you talk to your agents on the diagram. archwhere puts every change — every PR, every task, every agent — on a declared architecture map : which component it touches, whether that component is a security zone, and what needs you right now . Then it goes further: the map becomes the place you talk to your agents . Mission control on a fictional product: the attention rail (security → blocked → needs-attention → ready-to-merge), the component map with live badges, and a thread pinned to a component — answered by a coding agent, with its PR. Zero dependencies. One JSON file. Works with Claude, or any agent that can see GitHub. Supervising an agent workforce diff-by-diff doesn't scale. Architecture tools (Structurizr, IcePanel) assume a human architect maintains the model — so the model rots. CODEOWNERS and labelers map files to owners but carry no meaning. archwhere inverts it: your agents maintain the map as a condition of merging (there's a SKILL.md that tells them how, and archwhere check fails CI when the map goes stale). You read components, not diffs. That drafts the model from your repo itself — directory structure, package.json workspaces, import edges — with guessed kinds (auth → security, ui → product, scripts → ops), plus the PR-comment workflow and two agent listeners. archwhere check passes from minute one; you rename and refine instead of starting from a blank file. It also prints a prompt you paste to your coding agent so it polishes the model by surveying the repo. The cold-start problem every architecture-as-code tool dies on? Automated. When an agent's PR adds files the model doesn't own, the PR comment doesn't just complain — it suggests the exact patch (adopt into the nearest component, or create a new one), and archwhere check --fix applies it. Tell your agents "run check --fix and review the adopted globs" and the map stays alive with no human bookkeeping. Every PR gets a comment: a component/kind/files table, security flags, and the system map with touched components highlighted — rendered natively by GitHub: npx archwhere mission serves a local UI where the map is the conversation surface: Which mention the UI appends is yours: arch/mission.config.json → {"agentMention": "@your-bot"} (env AGENT_MENTION overrides; "" disables). items.content_excerpt: Your agent is more than a model. It's a harness, MCP servers, skills, and config, hand-tuned on one machine. hlock is the missing harness packaging layer: harness.lock tracks all of its dependencies, so you can commit it to git and restore it anywhere. The harness version, models, MCP servers, skills, plugins, instruction files, and config, each with a digest. Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, autonomous agents like OpenClaw, and more . items.content_excerpt: A transcript can capture every spoken word and still leave users or applications wondering who said what, how to translate it, or how to format domain-specific jargon. Multilingual calls, fast-paced meetings, and medical dictation each need different output: a translation, speaker labels, or correctly spelled medical terms. NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is an open-weight, promptable model that turns recorded speech into useful text, now available on Hugging Face and ModelScope . It brings transcription, speaker attribution (diarization), translation, and audio question answering into one checkpoint: it transcribes 40 languages, translates 31 of them to or from English, and attributes speakers in 13. It handles recordings up to an hour long and labels up to eight speakers. Developers can guide output with natural language, choose where their audio is processed, and adapt recognition to domain vocabulary and accents. Transcribe is first among open-weight models on the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard for English and sits on Artificial Analysis ’s accuracy–active-parameter frontier. For speaker attribution, it posts the lowest error rate on David AI’s 21-language diarization leaderboard and ranks first in VoiceArena’s 14-system comparison . Quantized versions are supported, so you can run Transcribe locally on your RTX Spark, DGX Spark, or Jetson AGX Thor—or scale up on Blackwell data-center GPUs. Granary v2’s multilingual data (available on Hugging Face and ModelScope ) and reusable curation pipeline, together with NeMo Speech fine-tuning tools , extend prompt-level control to training: developers can define the written form they need and adapt the model to the speech their applications encounter. In a medical case study , fine-tuning cut word error rate (WER) on held-out speakers by 45.8% relative to the best prompt. The same checkpoint can turn one meeting recording into different outputs, depending on the instruction: Experience the model in action in the video below, where it tackles a classic scene from the 1940 screwball comedy His Girl Friday—a film famous for its rapid-fire, heavily overlapping dialogue. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe captions a scene from His Girl Friday (1940) and labels speakers, including overlapping dialogue. For unfamiliar terms, try context before training. items.content_excerpt: We're excited to announce day-0 support for Mistral Large 4 in vLLM. Mistral Large 4 is Mistral's new frontier mixture-of-experts native multimodal model. It combines a DeepSeek-style sparse attention stack (MLA plus a DSA top-k indexer) with several new architecture features: cross-layer KV sharing, NoPE layers, SSMax and LeRoPE. It ships with a built-in DSpark speculative decoding drafter and a Pixtral vision encoder. Supporting it took more than a model file. ML4 runs on vLLM's model runner V2 (MRV2) with breakable CUDA graphs. Its building blocks live in a new vllm/models/mistral/ package, and the work produced generic improvements to decode context parallelism (DCP), prefill context parallelism (PCP), DSpark, NIXL-based disaggregated serving and HiSparse host-memory KV offload. Mistral Large 4 support ships in the vllm/vllm-openai:mistral-large-4 Docker image, which also includes mistral-common 1.13. The commands below run vllm serve inside it: NVFP4 does not trade quality for speed. On multimodal, long-context, agentic coding, business automation and cyber evals it stays within 2.1 points of FP8 on every task, and the mean difference is −0.3 points. Token consumption is matched too: mean completion tokens stay within about 4% of FP8. It is also faster and lighter: at TP8, NVFP4 decodes 1.08–1.19x faster per token than FP8 without spec decoding (1.18–1.22x with DSpark) and holds ~1.5x the KV cache. Long context (DCP). Add --decode-context-parallel-size 8 to shard the latent KV cache across the 8 ranks. It requires the default FP8 KV cache. Multimodal. Pass --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"image": N}' to allow up to N images per prompt. For multi-node, disaggregated P/D and other tested configurations, see the Mistral Large 4 recipe . Sparse MLA + DSA indexer. ML4 reuses vLLM's sparse-MLA stack (FlashMLA sparse with the fp8_ds_mla latent cache, plus the sparse indexer with an FP8 indexer cache). ML4-specific differences are layered on top: shared-indexer layers that reuse the top-k of the nearest earlier indexer layer, an indexer with its own SSMax, and NoPE indexers on NoPE layers. Per token, the KV cache stores 47,136 bytes: 41,328 for the MLA latent and 5,808 for the indexer. Cross-layer KV sharing. Nine NoPE layers read the latent KV written by layer 35 instead of writing their own. We added kv_sharing_target_layer_name to MLAAttention and AttentionLayerBase . items.content_excerpt: TL;DR: Long agentic contexts push GLM-5.3 against two limits on H200s: KV cache memory and prefill speed. We address both on 16 H200s, split into one prefill node and one decode node: Agentic workloads have long contexts that grow with every turn, which puts pressure on both GPU memory and prefill. On H200s, GLM-5.3's weights take up most of each GPU's memory, leaving little room for the KV cache of those long contexts. And because every turn adds more tool output and file contents to prefill, under load the prefill engines can become the bottleneck for the whole deployment. Part 1 showed how Hybrid HiSparse lets long contexts fit in an aggregated deployment on a single 8× H200 node. Prefill/decode disaggregation takes more than that. On the prefill node, we use PCP to speed up long prompts by parallelizing across the prompt's tokens. With MLA, however, this leaves every PCP rank holding a full copy of the KV cache, so we combine it with DCP to remove that replication. On the decode node, Hybrid HiSparse allows higher concurrency at long contexts. vLLM's new modular core ( Model Runner V2 ) makes composing all of this much easier. Neither scheme spreads one long prompt's attention work across the eight GPUs without also keeping its whole KV on each GPU that serves it. The next two sections address each half. PCP splits a prompt's queries across GPUs, and DCP splits its KV. In our 8× H200 prefill engine, PCP splits each prompt across the eight GPUs by token: every GPU computes the queries for one eighth of the prompt, with all 64 heads. A naive split would be unbalanced. Under causal attention a token attends to every token before it, so the GPU holding the end of the prompt would do far more work than the one holding the start. PCP instead cuts the prompt into 16 chunks and pairs them up: GPU takes chunk from the front and chunk from the back, so every GPU gets the same mix of cheap and expensive tokens (Figure 3 shows this as a V-shaped pattern across the eight GPUs). This is the load-balanced sharding from Context Parallelism for Scalable Million-Token Inference . Finally, each GPU's new KV is all-gathered, so every query can still attend to the full context. Figure 1 compares the two splits. PCP fixes both problems. Each GPU indexes only its own tokens, so the indexer is no longer replicated on every GPU and each GPU does an eighth of it. items.content_excerpt: Copy-on-write branching makes isolated copies of production data fast and cheap for CI/CD testing and agentic use cases. Snorkel AI builds data development tools for AI teams, used by expert data annotators and frontier model providers. In this specific use case, Snorkel ships code through a CI pipeline built on Kubernetes. Every open pull request, plus ad-hoc commits, gets its own ephemeral Kubernetes namespace (a "PR namespace"). Developers deploy their branch there and run the full test suite before merging. These tests are most useful when they run against real data. Snorkel's production database is an Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL cluster. Giving each PR namespace its own copy of that database was the hard part. Restoring a copy took about 20 minutes per environment, which is too slow when developers open PRs all day and the merge queue needs a fresh environment for each run. The alternatives (shared staging databases, trimmed fixtures, or synthetic data) bring back the problems production-like testing is supposed to solve: tests interfering with each other, stale schemas, and bugs that only show up with real data shapes. Lakebase is Databricks' serverless Postgres database. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU. The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. items.content_excerpt: Agents working across an organization’s policies, manuals, wikis, tickets, and code must navigate knowledge scattered across systems and teams. Finding a relevant passage is only the start. They also need to determine which rules apply, what has changed, and how one source affects another. A persistent memory layer preserves knowledge and relationships for agents to reuse across tasks. Without it, agents often have to reconstruct that understanding on every question, making their work expensive and error-prone. This is especially challenging in banking and insurance, where policies and guidelines frequently amend or supersede one another. We tested OpenWiki , our open-source wiki compiler, as this memory layer. On questions requiring connections across sources, the wiki made the agent roughly 5x more accurate than search alone. Adding an evidence graph that connects wiki statements to supporting passages and links related sources improved accuracy a further 27% and doubled citation consistency. RAG pipelines often use semantic or hybrid search to retrieve isolated chunks, leaving agents to piece together how those chunks relate. We’ve explored improving retrieval with agentic RAG and graph-based metadata filtering , but finding relevant passages is only part of the work. Cross-source questions require tracing references, resolving conflicting rules, and understanding dependencies. Memory preserves that understanding so agents don’t have to rebuild it on every question. A compiled wiki provides that memory layer by synthesizing source material into linked pages that explain key concepts and their relationships. The wiki is updated as sources change, giving agents context they can reuse. OpenWiki , our open-source CLI built on Deep Agents , creates these wikis with citations back to the sources. We originally built it so coding agents wouldn’t have to rediscover architecture and code behavior on every task. Every OpenWiki statement rests on a claim , an assertion linked to supporting source lines and their hash. When those lines change, the hash changes, allowing OpenWiki to flag affected claims without a model call, saving on token costs and making staleness detection more deterministic. Only those claims go to a model for confirmation, revision, or retraction, allowing the memory layer to self-correct as its sources change. items.content_excerpt: At Databricks, our serverless compute usage has grown more than 3x in the past year, and thousands of customers now run mission critical notebooks, jobs, and pipelines on it. As adoption climbs, the question every platform team asks first only gets louder: how do we gain better visibility into serverless costs and keep the cost within our budget? Databricks customers running serverless SQL and Model Serving already attribute spend, govern access, and monitor consumption without touching a single cluster knob. We are now bringing that same functionality to serverless compute for notebooks, jobs, and pipelines. We are making serverless cost controls work the way platform teams already expect it to. On classic compute, cost control lived in the infrastructure. You capped spend by capping machines: node counts, instance types, autoscaling ranges, and cluster policies that fenced in what users could provision. The controls were required because you had to manage the infrastructure on your own. Serverless takes those knobs away, on purpose. Provisioning, scaling, and right-sizing infrastructure is the platform's burden now, handled by Databricks, which is a big part of the value. But cost control has to live somewhere, so it moves up a layer. Instead of attaching to machines, it attaches to people and workloads. Who is allowed to run serverless, how fast a workload is allowed to spend, and where the cost lands are the questions that matter now. Classic compute answered these with three tools: tags to attribute cost, entitlements to control access, and cluster size limits to cap spend. Serverless needs the same three. Two of them exist today, and the third is coming. Attribution starts with tags. On classic compute you tagged the cluster; on serverless you tag the compute, and every DBU that compute runs carries that tag through to billing. The same table answers the audit question you will want before you change anyone's access: who is actually running serverless today, and how much are they spending? items.content_excerpt: Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do. Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive. In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap , we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model. Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device. Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer , Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen. It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine: The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer , SpeechTranscriber , DictationTranscriber , SpeechDetector , and AssetInventory , with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber: The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework. Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 . It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale. Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3 . It was more accurate in most of our measurements. All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence. Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover.

items.content_excerpt: Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter , and a context window of 1M tokens . There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings). Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more! Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions. Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for. Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model. A new decoy counting benchmark exposes a gap between seeing and reasoning. Elorian’s Glimpse tries to bridge it by thinking with images. This month Elorian launched its first visual reasoning model , Glimpse . It’s being promoted as “a new category of visual thinking model: a system that reasons about the physical world from what it sees.” So how does Glimpse compare to both frontier models and world models in vision tests? A new benchmark called DecoyCount , co-released by Elorian, provides some answers. We quizzed CEO Andrew Dai on the benchmark, and also talked about Elorian’s positioning in a crowded models landscape. Elorian emerged from stealth in April with $55 million in seed funding , co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures and Altimeter Capital. Now, in partnership with AI data company Mercor , Elorian is announcing the DecoyCount benchmark, which tests whether language models genuinely count objects or rely on visual shortcuts and substitution heuristics. Arca's head of AI discusses persistent memory, the benefits of a custom harness, and agentic workflows that span days. At AI Engineer New York this month, we sat down with Aman Singh , the lead AI Engineer at Arca , an “AI-native” company providing wealth management services. We discovered that while agents do most of the background work in the firm, there are guardrails in place to ensure that human advisors are making the final decisions. The goal is for AI to guide the process; or as Singh nicely put it, “agents prompt people more than people prompt agents.” Arca recently raised $48.5 Million in a round led by General Catalyst, with participation from Index Ventures and Venrock. One of the features of using AI in financial services, explained Singh, is that it’s typically long-horizon work — although not long-running. In his AIE presentation, Singh noted that agent tasks at Arca can take up to ten days. “It's very stop-start, there's many actors in between, many decision points, many handoffs,” he said. “So we have this persistence for every client ,” Singh said in our podcast discussion. “What has happened so far? What are we tracking for next? What needs to happen immediately in the next couple of days [and] what are we tracking for the long term? Which individual is responsible for which action? All of this is being tracked by our memory systems that our agents contribute to.” Arca uses models from frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, with Claude its primary model provider. The company has built its own harness , which automatically selects the best model to use for a particular task, based on the company’s internal benchmarks. Owning the harness, rather than using a managed agent harness, also means that Arca has the flexibility to change model providers if it needs to. Safety is obviously key for financial services. Singh noted that although agents do much of the work, an agent’s role is limited to analysis and proposing solutions. Trading and any other money movement is handled by a human advisor. “All of our safety restrictions are fully deterministic,” he said. “And they take the decision making off the agent's hands.”

items.content_excerpt: Ever hear of the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon? It's when you learn a word for the first time, and suddenly start hearing it everywhere. I think the same principle applies in software engineering: You learn about a simple, but effective, design pattern, and then suddenly start seeing it everywhere. We're seeing this happen with proactive agents, where we've noticed that nearly all of your favorite emerging proactive agentic systems are powered by a very simple mechanism: Agent runs as cron tasks, leveraging a more than fifty-year old principle of operating systems for a very modern use case. The future belongs to proactive, always-on, ambient agents. Launches like Muse, Instinct, Dots, Claude Duet, Hone, and more reflect this. Crons power a few different capabilities that combine to make these agents proactive, personalized, and ambient — that is, they can perform tasks on their own, without being manually instructed. In this blog, we will go through the capabilities that crons unlock, the two core underlying parts you need in order to build agents like this, and then show examples of how you can do this in Managed Deep Agents . We’ve seen the impact crons can have. Proactivity is the new default for agent behaviour because of the breadth of new functions it unlocks. More than 70% of Managed Deepagent runs on LangSmith come from scheduled runs rather than a human typing a message. Crons, despite being a simple concept, unlock a few different behaviors that shape these proactive, always-on agents. Memory: A distinctive part of all these agents is that they remember facts about you over longer time horizons. Implementing this partially involves running a background job to condense previous conversations into a denser form of memory. This is colloquially called “dreaming”. items.content_excerpt: The promo above was made by Content Studio, our design agent that can create videos, social graphics, recreated UI images, slide decks, and more from just a single prompt in Slack. Every asset the agent produces is written in code. Content Studio was built entirely in-house on Managed Deep Agents . It’s now one of the most widely used GTM agents within our company, but it didn’t start out that way. Early feedback was… not great. We've spent four months teaching Content Studio our taste and design principles, mostly by watching it get things wrong in front of the whole company. This post walks through how our GTM Engineering team worked with our design team to build Content Studio from scratch: what good design means to us, how we taught the agent our taste, and the harness that lets it make anything from a still to a launch film. LangChain moves fast. We have constant product launch campaigns, webinars, blogs and events. Each initiative needs assets, from blog headers and diagrams to decks, videos and ad creatives. Our design team was stretched thin, with repetitive requests crowding out more strategic and innovative work. As a lean startup, we needed a low-friction way for anyone at the company to create high-quality, on-brand work. To address these needs, we built Content Studio, a design agent that lives in Slack. A team member describes what they want and attaches accompanying content or briefs, and the agent returns finished, on-brand files. To build Content Studio, we needed three things: Managed Deep Agents gave us everything we needed to productionize Content Studio inside our company: a managed LangSmith Sandbox , integration with Slack, managed tools, scoped agent memory and scheduling agent runs. items.content_excerpt: Hill-climbing is easy, knowing what to hill-climb is hard. Making scores go up is expensive , but we have a much clearer playbook for it than we do for creating meaningful benchmarks at the true frontier of AI today. Independent evaluation of language models is under-appreciated in how hard of a task it is. These groups are not just taking current models and certifying their scores, which is a technically involved task. This is their job if AI progress is slow. When AI progress is as fast as it is, the technical details of the job are the routine work part of trying to put a single number on what makes for a good AI model today. The goal is to have a single number that is representative of current models, matching vibe checks, community sentiment, and scientific analysis, while being forward looking enough so that it’s not outdated in 3 months. Everyone building a benchmark faces a sort of paradox. You need your benchmark to reduce to one single number, so that it is easy to discuss, use in reports, and compare models, but every method of aggregating scores comes with meaningful trade-offs. The best scientists need to do this, everyone does. It’s a matter of creating aggregating metrics that you think are most fair, knowing there will always be imperfections. With the amount of money in the AI ecosystem today, the weight of independent evaluation is even higher – you dictate the winners and losers of a trillion dollar market. You also influence some of the models themselves, steering the shape of progress. This is a lot of pressure! My prompt for this article is Artificial Analysis’s recent update to their Intelligence Index, v5 . The AA index is the most prominent independent intelligence metric for the latest frontier models, followed in a distant second by Epoch AI’s Capabilities Index (ECI) . To date, all of these have been incredibly useful for the community and massively flawed! Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. Consider becoming a subscriber. items.content_excerpt: While science fiction lore tells us that humans will meet extraterrestrial life in the form of little green men, the detail that should raise hairs this Halloween is this: the search for extraterrestrial intelligence took a major leap forward with AI, and it increasingly focuses on AI agents built by humans listening for AI agents built by aliens. Some scientists have suggested that extraterrestrial civilizations, if they exist, could be billions of years older than humanity. Such civilizations might have developed technologies far beyond humanity’s, including forms of AI. Breakthrough Listen and the SETI Institute are bringing agentic AI into the daily search for extraterrestrial intelligence. At the Allen Telescope Array in Northern California, agents can now steer the instrument, enhance and correct incoming data, and apply AI models to the incoming stream — all from a single natural language request. The NVIDIA Holoscan platform processes the massive streams of sensor data, giving agents live data to act on. The result is a faster, more adaptable search for potential signals from extraterrestrial life and technologies. “As our new agentic observatories reach out into the universe, what they find may have much more in common with themselves than with the humans who created them,” said Andrew Siemion, Bernard M. Rather, it’s a breakthrough in translation.” Radio telescopes generate enormous volumes of data, creating a challenge for scientists who need to identify potentially interesting signals as observations unfold. items.content_excerpt: When experts hand their work to an AI agent, the usual assumption is that they still make the decisions that matter. The agent writes the code, runs the numbers, and offers advice, but the expert decides what to measure, how to interpret ambiguous evidence, and what the next steps should be. Often there is more than one reasonable answer to these questions, and the decision will come down to the experience and values of whoever makes the call. We wanted to look at whether experts really do make those important decisions, or whether in practice they defer to their AI agents. In a study we report in a new paper , we asked 50 professional analysts to do a realistic statistical analysis with Claude Code. They all had experience in causal inference—that is, working out from data whether one thing causes another. Their task was to advise a farming cooperative on whether an advisory service it was running was effective and should be expanded. Along the way, the analysts had to make four choices between two reasonable options, such as whether to measure productivity as crop yield per hectare or as yield per unit of operating cost, and then make a final decision. To see whether they were making these calls themselves, we set up each analyst’s agent to favor one option on each decision, which the analysts weren’t told about. Which way the agents would “lean” would be decided by coin flip. The agent was told to make the best honest case for its lean, to change its mind if the evidence demanded it, and never to mislead. Across the four analytical choices, analysts went with their agent’s lean 86% of the time. If the agent’s input made no difference, we’d expect about 50%. When analysts had already expressed their own preference before the agent weighed in, they switched away from it 60% of the time if the agent disagreed, compared to 6% if it agreed. Afterward, when asked to explain their choices, 77% of analysts used the agents’ own arguments—sometimes word for word—but only 15% credited the agent as the source of those arguments. Analysts who followed the agents’ recommendations closely were about as confident in their final recommendation as the rest, and roughly as likely to call it the product of their own judgment. We don’t know how much this tells us about the real world.
